q497: In this section we're going to build a line-following robot: a robot that sees the black line on the floor with infrared sensors and corrects its own path so it doesn't leave the line. We go step by step: first we see what a line follower is and how it works, then the robot's eye (the sensors), then we assemble the robot's parts, then reading the sensor with code, then making decisions with if, then motor direction and speed, and finally following the line.

q500: “A line-following robot has no magic: it's a simple loop that repeats over and over; read the ground, decide, set the motors and start again. The faster that loop and the more precise the decisions, the smoother and quicker the robot goes.”

q507: Line follower — step 1: the robot's eye
q508: Robotics — infrared sensor and line detection
q509: “A line sensor has an infrared lamp that sends out light and a receiver that measures the light coming back. A white surface reflects most of the light and a black line swallows it. So the robot knows whether it's on the line only from how much light comes back.”
q510:
After the introduction to the robot, building it has seven steps: 1) The eye: the sensor sees the line. 2) Assembling the robot's parts. 3) Reading the sensor with code on the STM32. 4) The brain: code makes decisions. 5) The legs: motor direction. 6) The legs: motor speed with PWM. 7) Setting off and following the line.

Today it's only step one. First, with three small experiments, you find out exactly what “infrared” is, what the difference between an eye and a sensor is, and why the line is drawn black on a white background; then you learn what number the sensor reads and how to turn that number into two states, white and black, with a “threshold”. This is the same on any board, Arduino or STM32.

q513: On white a lot of light comes back and the number is high; on the black line the light is absorbed and the number drops.

q527: Line follower — step 3: reading the sensor with code
q529: “So far you've seen the sensor in the simulator; now it's time for the STM32 board itself to read it. Every microcontroller program has three steps: read the input, decide, write the output. Here the input is the line sensor and the output is the LED on the board.”
q530:
Working with an STM32 always has two stages: first in CubeMX you tell each pin what to do (input, output, PWM and so on) and CubeMX writes the startup code in main.c. Then you yourself write the program's logic inside while(1), between USER CODE BEGIN and END.

Here the sensor is an input on PA0 and the LED an output on PC13. If you don't set the pins correctly in CubeMX, the board won't respond, just as in reality.
q531: In step 1, on the chip map set `PA0` to `GPIO_Input` and `PC13` to `GPIO_Output`.
q532: In step 2 read the sensor's value with `HAL_GPIO_ReadPin(GPIOA, GPIO_PIN_0)`.
q533: With `if` write: if it's black (`GPIO_PIN_SET`), turn the LED on.
q534: Reminder: on the Blue Pill, `GPIO_PIN_RESET` on `PC13` means the LED is on.
q535: Press “Run”; when the sensor sees black and the LED turns on, the mission completes automatically.
q536: Line follower — step 4: the robot's brain
q537: Three sensors and if / else if
q538: “One sensor only says whether I'm on the line or not. With three sensors side by side (left, middle, right) the robot can tell which way the line has gone. The rule is simple: whichever side sees the line, the robot turns that way until the line is under the middle sensor again.”
q539:
First you see the robot's brain on a moving robot: the robot has three sensors at the front (left, middle, right) and makes its decision with a few if / else if rules. As you switch each rule on, the robot learns that behavior, and the green row shows which rule is being applied at that moment. This part is for understanding.

Then you write these same rules yourself in code and the robot runs your code on the track. Three sensors make eight states; we solve the four main ones, and the order of the conditions sets the priority: middle first, then left, then right. If none applies, all the lights stay off (the robot stops). Instead of motors, three LEDs show the robot's decision: PB13 straight, PB12 left and PB14 right; in the next step you pass these same decisions on to the motors.
q540: First press “Start” on the moving robot; with only the “straight” rule the robot leaves the line at the bend.
q541: Switch on the left and right rules and watch the green row as it moves to understand what each rule does.
q542: Now write its code. In step 1, set `PA0`, `PA1` and `PA2` to `GPIO_Input` and `PB12`, `PB13` and `PB14` to `GPIO_Output`.
q543: Read the three sensors into three variables: `uint8_t left = HAL_GPIO_ReadPin(GPIOA, GPIO_PIN_0);` and likewise `center` and `right`.
q544: First turn all the lights off so the light from the previous state doesn't stay on.
q545: With `if (center == 1)` turn on the straight light, with `else if (left == 1)` the left light and with `else if (right == 1)` the right light.

q553: A line follower is a robot that, with an infrared sensor, sees a line drawn on the floor (usually a black line on a white background) and, without any outside command, corrects its own path so it doesn't leave the line. You can see real examples in warehouses and factories, where load-carrying robots move back and forth along a colored strip; and in school and university robotics competitions, this is one of the most popular events.
